Preview is read-only. It lists the files a restore would replace, and nothing on disk changes.

The restore overwrites every file on that list with the backup copy, including any local file that's newer than the backup. Those newer versions are gone unless you copied them somewhere first. Use the preview to see what's about to get clobbered, not to keep it safe.

Our release has two steps: upload the new assets under new versioned names, then switch the manifest to point at them. The old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest switch is the moment browsers start asking for the new names. If any of those files weren't uploaded yet, browsers would get 404s and the page would break. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists before anyone can see the manifest. Because the names are versioned, the upload doesn't overwrite anything the current site uses, so it's invisible to users until the switch. The switch itself is then the single step that changes what users get.

**Why we keep the old assets:** A browser that already fetched the previous manifest, such as an open tab, keeps requesting the old names, for example when it loads a chunk or image later in the session. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would hit 404s partway through using the site. Keeping them means each browser always gets a complete, matching set of files, either all old or all new, never a mix.

Our static-site release has two steps, in a fixed order.

First, we upload every new asset under a versioned name, so a new file never overwrites an existing one. Second, we switch the manifest to point at the new names. The manifest is what tells a browser which asset files to load.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest switch is the moment a release goes live. Once it happens, any browser that fetches the manifest immediately requests the files it names. If we switched first, some of those files might not be uploaded yet, and those browsers would get missing assets and a broken page. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names already exists when anyone can see it. The switch becomes a single cutover, and nobody ever sees a half-released site.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch still holds the old file names and will keep requesting them for the rest of that session. If we deleted the old files at release time, those browsers would start failing in the middle of a session. Leaving them in place lets those visitors keep working on the old version until they next load the manifest and move to the new one. Because the names are versioned, both sets of files can sit side by side without conflict.

Our static-site release has two steps, in this order:

1. Upload every new asset under a new versioned name.
2. Switch the manifest to point at those new names.

Old assets are not deleted when the manifest switches.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest tells the browser which asset files to load. If we switched the manifest before the new assets existed, any browser that fetched it in that window would request files that aren't there yet and get broken pages. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already exists the moment the manifest goes live. Because the new assets use new names, uploading them doesn't touch anything the current manifest references, so live traffic is unaffected until the switch.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. Those browsers will keep requesting assets by the old names, for example when they lazy-load a script or route to a new page. If we removed the old assets, those requests would fail and users mid-session would hit errors. Keeping the old assets lets those sessions finish on the version they started with, while new visitors get the new manifest and the new assets.

Our static-site releases happen in two steps: upload, then switch.

1. **Upload.** Every new asset goes up under a versioned name, so it never overwrites an existing file.
2. **Switch.** We update the manifest to point at the new names. This is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest is what browsers follow. If it pointed at the new names before those files existed, any browser that fetched it in that window would request assets that aren't there yet and get a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references is already available when it goes live. That makes the switch a single, clean cutover.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the page before the switch is still working from the previous manifest. It will keep requesting the old versioned names, for example when it lazy-loads a script or fetches an image later. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would hit missing assets mid-session. Because the versioned names differ, old and new assets can sit side by side without conflict, so keeping the old ones costs us nothing in correctness.
